title: Conservatives push for ethics review of Ottawa’s $1.6-billion Cohere investment
html:
Management consultant Dominic Barton was appointed in August as board chair of Invest in Canada.Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press

The Conservatives are seeking an ethics committee review of the government’s $1.6-billion investment in AI firm Cohere and potential conflicts of interest involving two private-sector leaders who have financial ties to the company and have been recently appointed to senior government roles.

The Official Opposition gave notice of a motion Wednesday evening at the Commons ethics committee calling for a study.

It calls on the committee to hear from several people, including international management consultant Dominic Barton, who was appointed in August as board chair of Invest in Canada, an investment promotion agency. It also names Patrick Pichette, a former Google executive who was appointed in September as head of Ottawa’s new digital transformation agency. Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon is also requested to appear. The motion will be put to a vote at a future meeting.

Both Mr. Barton and Mr. Pichette have links to Cohere, the Toronto-based AI company that Prime Minister Mark Carney announced last month will receive the federal financing. It marked a rare example of Ottawa taking a direct equity stake in a private company, as opposed to simply providing loans or grants.

The call for a study follows Mr. Pichette’s first committee appearance last week as head of Digital Transformation Canada, which will take over responsibilities for government-wide technology from Shared Services Canada, as well as some functions from other departments.

During the Nov. 19 meeting of the government operations committee, Mr. Pichette faced several Conservative questions about his financial ties to Cohere and Inovia Capital, an investor in Cohere.

Former Google executive Patrick Pichette was appointed in September as head of Ottawa’s new digital transformation agency.PATRICK DOYLE/The Canadian Press

Mr. Pichette is a former board member of Cohere. He was also a partner at Montreal-based Inovia Capital. He told MPs last week that he did not know if he continues to have a financial interest in the company.

“I have no clue if I have an interest, today, given that I am in the process of setting up a blind trust under the Ethics Commissioner. I’m just following all their steps,” Mr. Pichette told MPs.

When asked again if he has fully divested from Inovia Capital, Mr. Pichette did not answer directly.

“I’m going to answer with the following: I took this job for a dollar a year,” he said. “They gave me a stipend, which I’m going to give to charity. I’m working for free. I don’t think I’m here to make money. That would be my answer on the record.”

Mr. Pichette is a former member of the federal government’s AI Strategy Task Force, launched in September 2025.

He provided a written submission to the task force last year as an individual. He declared in that report that he had a conflict of interest in light of his investment and board seat in Cohere and ties to other companies.

“This conflict is the result of my firm investing in Canadian leading companies, so should not come as a surprise to anyone,” he wrote.

Of his five main recommendations in his submission, one included: “Declare Cohere our National LLM [Large Language Model] Champion, and fuel it with large revenue contracts to support our data sovereignty, reinvent our federal services, and support its international expansion.”

He also called for Canada to become a world leader in low-cost, safe data centre infrastructure and to “reform the pension funds to ensure they invest a minimum of our 5% of assets in Canadian tech priorities and next-generation deep tech industries.”

Conservative MP and procurement critic Dan Mazier said that while Mr. Pichette may not be collecting a salary, he could potentially benefit from government decisions through his investments. He also said the rules related to a blind trust are not clear.

“We need some transparency here,” he said in an interview. “It just reeks.”

During a Nov. 17 appearance before the Commons trade committee, Mr. Barton was asked about his connections to Cohere. Mr. Barton spent nearly 30 years with the global consulting firm McKinsey, and also served as Canada’s ambassador to China.

He said he is a partner in a venture capital firm called Radical Ventures, which was an early investor in Cohere.

Conservative MP Jacob Mantle asked Mr. Barton how the government’s $1.6-billion funding announcement affected his investment in the company.

“No idea,” Mr. Barton replied. “I‘m not involved in any of the particular investments in my role at Radical, so I have no detail on that whatsoever.”

On Tuesday, Mr. Mazier moved a motion at the government operations committee asking that it report a potential breach of privilege to the House of Commons. The motion said Mr. Pichette refused to answer some questions, was at times evasive and made contradictory claims during his appearance last week.

The Bloc supported the motion, but it was defeated in a 5-4 vote by the Liberal majority on the committee.

Liberal MP and committee member John-Paul Danko said the debate would be better placed before the ethics committee.

“I think that would be an appropriate place or appropriate venue for a further review, if that’s deemed necessary by that committee,” Mr. Danko said Tuesday. He then declined when Mr. Mazier asked if he would support sending a letter to the ethics committee asking them to study the matter.
summary: Review would also probe potential conflicts of interest involving two private-sector leaders who have financial ties to the AI company
